title: The Mind–Body Problem
description: How does the mind relate to the body? Dualism and its discontents

concepts.title: Substance Dualism
concepts.contentHtml:
Descartes argued that mind and body are two fundamentally distinct substances: res cogitans (thinking substance, the mind) and res extensa (extended substance, the body).

The mind is indivisible, non-spatial, and known with certainty. The body is spatial, divisible, and known only probabilistically. They interact via the pineal gland — a hypothesis now considered false.

The central problem with dualism is causal interaction: how can a non-physical mind cause physical arm movements, and how can physical events (a pin prick) cause non-physical pain? This interaction problem haunts all forms of substance dualism.

concepts.title: Varieties of Monism
concepts.contentHtml:
Most contemporary philosophers reject substance dualism in favour of monism — the view that there is only one kind of substance.

Physicalism (materialism): everything that exists is physical or fully depends on the physical. The mind is what the brain does. This is the dominant view in contemporary philosophy of mind and cognitive science.

Idealism: only minds and mental contents genuinely exist; physical reality is constructed from or reducible to mental items. Berkeley: 'esse est percipi' — to be is to be perceived.

Neutral monism (Russell, Spinoza in a different form): the fundamental substance is neither mental nor physical; mind and matter are two aspects of the same underlying reality.

concepts.title: Property Dualism
concepts.contentHtml:
Property dualism avoids substance dualism's interaction problem while preserving the intuition that mental properties are genuinely distinct.

Property dualists hold that there is one kind of substance (physical) but two kinds of properties: physical properties (mass, charge) and mental properties (the feel of pain, the redness of a seen colour).

Mental properties are not reducible to physical properties, even if they depend on them.

Epiphenomenalism (Huxley): mental events are byproducts of physical brain events but have no causal power. Consciousness is like steam from a train — it accompanies the engine but doesn't drive it. Critics: if consciousness is causally inert, why did it evolve?

title: Functionalism and Physicalism
description: The mind as software: what mental states do, not what they are made of

concepts.title: Identity Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
The mind-brain identity theory (Place, Smart, Armstrong) holds that mental states are identical to brain states. Pain just is C-fibre firing; beliefs just are neural configurations.

This is a type identity theory: every mental type corresponds to a physical type. It is attractive because it respects the causal efficacy of mental states — they cause things because brain states cause things.

The main objection is multiple realisability (Putnam): pain in a human is C-fibre firing; pain in an octopus (no C-fibres) may be a completely different neural state; pain in a silicon robot might be a computational state. One mental type corresponds to many physical types. Type identity seems to rule out alien or artificial minds — implausibly.

concepts.title: Functionalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Functionalism responds to multiple realisability by defining mental states by their functional role — their causal relations to inputs, outputs, and other mental states — rather than their physical realisation.

Pain is whatever state is caused by tissue damage, causes aversive behaviour and belief that something is wrong, and motivates the desire to stop it — regardless of whether it is realised in neurons, silicon, or something else.

Hilary Putnam and Jerry Fodor developed functionalism in the 1960s-70s, making it the dominant view for decades. It naturally fits the computer metaphor: the mind is the software; the brain is the hardware.

Critics question whether functional role is sufficient to capture the phenomenal feel of experience — the classic 'inverted qualia' and 'absent qualia' problems.

concepts.title: The Chinese Room
concepts.contentHtml:
John Searle's Chinese Room argument (1980) attacks the claim that running the right program is sufficient for understanding or genuine mentality.

Imagine a person locked in a room following rules to manipulate Chinese symbols, producing outputs indistinguishable from a native speaker's. The person doesn't understand Chinese — yet the system passes any behavioural test.

Searle's conclusion: syntax is not sufficient for semantics. Running a program (formal symbol manipulation) cannot by itself produce genuine understanding or intentionality. Intentionality — mental states being about something — requires causal connections to the world, which programs lack.

Functionalists reply with the systems reply: the person doesn't understand, but the whole system (person + rules + symbols) does. Debate continues.

title: Consciousness and Qualia
description: What is it like to be something? The hard problem of consciousness

concepts.title: Qualia and Phenomenal Experience
concepts.contentHtml:
Qualia are the subjective, felt qualities of experience: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, the taste of coffee. The philosophical term for this is phenomenal consciousness or 'what it is like' (Nagel).

Thomas Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974) argued that bats have echolocation experiences we cannot imagine from the outside. Even complete physical knowledge about bat brains wouldn't tell us what their experience feels like.

This thought experiment isolates the subjective, first-person character of experience as something that resists third-person physical description. Qualia seem to be the explanatory target that physicalist theories of mind must account for — and many think they fail.

concepts.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
concepts.contentHtml:
David Chalmers (1995) distinguished the easy problems from the hard problem of consciousness.

Easy problems (not actually easy, but tractable in principle): explaining attention, memory, reportability, integration of information, sleep/waking differences. These are problems about cognitive functions — how the brain does things.

The hard problem: why is there subjective experience at all? Why does information processing feel like anything from the inside? Even a complete functional and neural account of the brain seems to leave this open. A philosophical zombie — physically identical to you but with no inner experience — seems conceivable. If so, physicalism cannot explain consciousness.

concepts.title: Physicalist Responses to the Hard Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
Physicalists have several responses to Chalmers:

Eliminativism (Dennett): qualia as traditionally conceived don't exist. 'Consciousness' is a confused folk concept — there are only brain processes. Heterophenomenology studies what subjects say about their experience without assuming the experiences are as they seem.

Higher-order theories (Rosenthal): a mental state is conscious when it is accompanied by a higher-order thought about that state. Phenomenal properties are real but reducible to functional/representational ones.

Illusionism (Frankish): phenomenal consciousness as conceived (non-physical qualia) is an introspective illusion. We are deceived about the nature of our own experience — mistaking functional states for something more.

title: Intentionality and Mental Content
description: How do mental states manage to be about things in the world?

concepts.title: Intentionality: The Mark of the Mental
concepts.contentHtml:
Franz Brentano (1874) claimed that intentionality — the directedness of mental states toward objects — is what distinguishes mental from physical phenomena. Beliefs, desires, fears, and hopes are always about something.

Physical states like rocks or rivers have no intentionality — a river doesn't flow toward the sea in the intentional sense. But my desire is intrinsically directed toward a goal; my belief is about Paris.

The puzzle: how does a physical brain state manage to be about Paris? What makes neurons 'represent' something rather than just cause something? This is the problem of mental content, sometimes called the problem of intentionality or representation.

concepts.title: Theories of Mental Content
concepts.contentHtml:
Several theories try to explain how mental states acquire content:

Causal/informational theories (Fodor, Dretske): mental representations mean what they are reliably caused by. 'Cow' thoughts are about cows because cows cause cow-thoughts. Problem: misrepresentation — if I see a horse in the dark and think 'cow', horses cause cow-thoughts; doesn't that make 'cow' mean horse?

Teleosemantic theories (Millikan): mental representations have content they are biologically designed (by natural selection) to indicate. Misrepresentation is when a mechanism fails to fulfil its biological function.

Interpretationism (Dennett): mental content is what a system would have to represent, given the most useful predictive interpretation of its behaviour — the intentional stance. No deeper fact about content exists.

concepts.title: Narrow vs Wide Content
concepts.contentHtml:
Hilary Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment (1975): your physical duplicate on Twin Earth drinks XYZ rather than H₂O, but both are called 'water.' You and your twin have identical brains, yet your 'water' thought refers to H₂O and your twin's to XYZ.

Putnam concluded: 'meanings ain't in the head.' The content of mental states is partly determined by the external environment — this is wide content (externalism about mental content).

Narrow content: the intrinsic computational/functional state, shared by you and your twin. Some argue narrow content is what's relevant to explaining behaviour. Others (Burge) extend externalism to social environment: 'arthritis' means what the community means by it, not what your individual brain state dictates.

title: Personal Identity, Self, and AI Minds
description: What makes you you? Can machines have minds?

concepts.title: The Narrative Self and Embodied Cognition
concepts.contentHtml:
Contemporary philosophy of mind has increasingly emphasised the role of the body and environment in constituting the mind.

Embodied cognition (Merleau-Ponty, Varela): cognition is not confined to the brain; it involves the whole organism and its environment. The body's sensorimotor capacities shape how the world is perceived and conceptualised.

The narrative self (Ricoeur, Schechtman): personal identity is not grounded in metaphysical substance or memory chains alone, but in the ongoing story we tell about ourselves. A life that coheres as a narrative is a unified self — even with gaps and inconsistencies. This connects philosophy of mind to questions of agency, responsibility, and psychological health.

concepts.title: The Turing Test and Machine Consciousness
concepts.contentHtml:
Alan Turing proposed in 1950 that if a machine can pass a behavioural indistinguishability test — conversing in natural language indistinguishably from a human — then we should attribute intelligence to it.

The Turing Test operationalises intelligence behaviourally, avoiding metaphysical questions about internal states. Critics (including Searle) argue it tests only behavioural mimicry, not genuine understanding or consciousness.

Contemporary large language models raise these questions acutely: they pass many Turing-style tests. Do they understand? Do they have any form of experience? The question splits philosophers. Functionalists who identify mind with functional organisation face pressure to say yes; those who require causal grounding in biological processes say no.

concepts.title: Panpsychism and the Future of Mind
concepts.contentHtml:
Frustrated by the hard problem's persistence, some philosophers have revisited panpsychism: the view that mentality or experience is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality.

Philip Goff argues that if physical descriptions always leave out the intrinsic nature of matter, and if consciousness is the one thing we know intrinsically, then consciousness (or proto-consciousness) may be the intrinsic nature of physical reality. Electrons don't experience richly — but they have some minimal form of inner existence.

Cosmopsychism (Shani, Goff): the cosmos as a whole is conscious; individual minds are derivations of its cosmic consciousness. This mirrors idealist traditions from Spinoza to Schelling.

Critics argue panpsychism faces the combination problem: how do micro-experiences combine into unified human consciousness?
